summary: Neurodegenerative disorders present one of the most challenging fronts in modern medicine, with diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease impacting millions globally. These conditions are characterized by the progressive degeneration and death of nerve cells, which is a complex interplay of genetic, oxidative, and inflammatory factors. The conventional therapeutic strategies are often inadequate, mainly due to their inability to target multiple pathological pathways simultaneously. As such, there is a critical need for innovative approaches that address these limitations effectively. In addition to central nervous system disorders, neurodegenerative conditions affecting the retina, such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and retinitis pigmentosa (RP), represent significant challenges. These retinal neurodegenerations share common pathological mechanisms with other neurodegenerative diseases, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic inflammation.

summary: The orexin/hypocretin system, first identified in 1998, is now recognized as a central regulator of energy balance, sleep–wake states, and arousal stability. Orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus integrate circadian, metabolic, and environmental signals to promote wakefulness and stabilize sleep–wake transitions. Beyond arousal regulation, orexin signaling plays a key role in hedonic and motivational processes, as these neurons densely innervate limbic and reward-related brain regions. Disruption of this system has been implicated in sleep disorders, including narcolepsy type 1, insomnia, and hypersomnia, as well as substance use disorders. Emerging evidence further links orexin dysfunction to neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative, and psychiatric conditions.

title: Transdiagnostic affective neuroscience: from negative affect to anhedonia and cognitive control.
summary: Research in psychiatry and clinical neuroscience is increasingly recognizing that negative affect and anhedonia are not confined to a single diagnostic category. Traditionally, most research on these symptoms has been conducted within single-diagnosis frameworks, treating depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and anxiety-related conditions as largely separate research literatures. This separation limits understanding of the shared neural and cognitive mechanisms that link reduced positive affect to impaired cognitive control across conditions. While several studies have pointed to overlapping reward and executive control circuits across diagnoses, critical questions remain about how these mechanisms interact, whether they follow a common trajectory, and how they can be reliably measured and targeted for intervention. title: Robotics & machine learning for understanding neural networks
summary: Biological neural networks are immensely complex systems underlying all aspects of cognition and behavior. Despite significant advances in neuroscience, a comprehensive understanding of their intricate computational principles remains a grand challenge. Concurrently, artificial neural networks (ANNs) and deep learning have revolutionized artificial intelligence, demonstrating impressive capabilities often inspired by biological architectures. However, translating insights from ANNs back to fundamental biological mechanisms is often non-trivial. Robotics offers a unique avenue to bridge this gap, providing embodied platforms to test computational models of neural function in dynamic, interactive environments. This Research Topic seeks to leverage the analytical power of machine learning and the experimental validation capabilities of robotics to gain deeper insights into the working principles of biological neural networks.

title: Virtual reality as a tool for cognitive and sensory modulation
summary: Virtual Reality (VR) has emerged as a transformative medium in neuroscience, moving beyond entertainment into a robust tool for experimental manipulation. Traditionally, studying cognitive and sensory processes required a trade-off between controlled laboratory settings and real-world ecological validity. VR bridges this gap by providing immersive, three-dimensional environments that can be precisely modulated to isolate specific neural responses. By engaging multiple sensory modalities—visual, auditory, and increasingly somatosensory—VR creates a sense of "presence" that activates the brain in ways traditional 2D stimuli cannot. This immersive capacity allows researchers to investigate how the human brain processes complex sensory inputs and orchestrates cognitive functions in real-time.

title: Mitophagy and Mitochondrial Quality Control in Brain Aging and Neurodegeneration
summary: Mitochondria are central to neuronal survival, synaptic function, and brain resilience across the lifespan. As the brain ages, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired mitophagy, and defects in mitochondrial quality control pathways emerge as key drivers of neurodegeneration. Disrupted clearance of damaged mitochondria contributes to oxidative stress, energy failure, inflammation, and protein aggregation, all of which are hallmarks of disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and other age-related cognitive and motor syndromes.

Approximately one in ten ischemic stroke victims also suffer from concurrent cancer, a statistic anticipated to increase with the advancements in cancer treatments that prolong survival. Recent studies reveal an emergence of stroke within two years of a cancer diagnosis in an additional 3-5% of cases. These include strokes that coincide with specific cancer therapies like chemotherapy and radiation, which could augment stroke risk through various mechanisms, including the induction of hypercoagulable states. Moreover, certain cancers have shown a high propensity to cause vascular complications, thus exacerbating the likelihood of stroke.

summary: Climate change and emerging environmental pollutants are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of mental health worldwide. Yet, while hospitals are becoming “smarter,” educational frameworks are often still playing catch-up. Proficiency with digital health tools is no longer a niche technical skill; it is a core clinical competency. However, many practitioners find themselves "learning on the fly", navigating complex systems and AI-generated insights without a formal roadmap. This Research Topic explores how we can move beyond fragmented, informal training and build a robust, evidence-based curriculum that prepares the next generation of clinicians to thrive in a technology-rich environment.

summary: Behavioral and psychiatric disorders arise from dynamic interactions between genetic predisposition and environmental influences across development and aging. Targeting Neuroinflammation in Spinal Cord Injury: From Inflammatory Mechanisms to Pharmacological Interventions
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a devastating secondary neuroinflammatory cascade—driven by microglial activation, immune infiltration, and sustained pro-inflammatory mediator release—that exacerbates tissue damage and impedes neurological recovery. The dynamic balance between pro-inflammatory (M1) and reparative (M2) phenotypes of microglia/macrophages has emerged as a critical determinant of injury outcome. Key signaling pathways, including NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, TLR4, and the CCL2/CCR2 axis, represent promising pharmacological targets. Despite encouraging preclinical advances, effective clinical translation remains limited. This Research Topic aims to bridge mechanistic insights into SCI neuroinflammation with innovative pharmacological interventions, fostering the development of targeted therapies that can ultimately improve functional recovery after SCI.

Brain Injury after Hypoxia/Ischemia: Mechanisms, Pathogenesis, and Potential Therapeutic Interventions
summary: Brain injury resulting from hypoxia (oxygen deprivation) or ischemia (restricted blood flow) represents a major challenge in medical research and clinical practice. Such injuries, often due to stroke, cardiac arrest, or asphyxiation, lead to significant consequences, including motor deficits, cognitive impairments, and increased mortality. The pathogenesis of these injuries involves a complex interplay of cellular and molecular events, including oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic disruptions, excitotoxicity, and apoptosis. A deep understanding of these mechanisms is essential for developing effective therapeutic interventions. This research topic aims to thoroughly investigate the mechanisms driving hypoxia/ischemia-induced brain injury and identify novel therapeutic strategies to mitigate damage, promoting neuronal recovery and survival.

title: Beyond Symptom Control - Mechanistic Lessons from Failed and Emerging Disease-Modifying Therapies in Parkinson’s Disease
summary: Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, yet despite decades of mechanistic insight, every clinical trial of a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) to date has failed to deliver unequivocal evidence of slowed neurodegeneration. Recent high-profile negative results — including trials of NLY01 (a GLP-1 receptor agonist targeting microglial activation) and deferiprone (an iron chelator targeting nigral iron accumulation and ferroptotic vulnerability) — have prompted a critical re-examination of the preclinical models, target validation strategies, and molecular hypotheses that underpin the DMT pipeline.

title: Social Isolation, Social Participation, and Health Outcomes in Older Adults
summary: Research on ageing populations increasingly highlights the profound effects of social connectedness on health and well-being in later life. Social isolation is recognized as a significant risk factor for a range of adverse health outcomes among older adults, including cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, depression, and reduced quality of life. While social participation is frequently associated with more positive physical and psychological outcomes, the mechanisms linking these factors remain insufficiently explored. The rapid uptake of digital technology, particularly smartphones, introduces both opportunities and challenges to the social integration of older people. Despite a growing body of research, much of the current literature is fragmented and lacks a holistic view of how overlapping social, technological, and psychological variables interact to shape health trajectories among older adults.

summary: The human brain is a relentless processor of sensory information, yet only a small fraction of this input reaches the level of conscious awareness. By precisely controlling stimulus properties, through techniques such as masking, binocular rivalry, or continuous flash suppression, researchers can dissociate physical input from subjective experience. Historically, we have known that the brain can perform complex tasks, such as emotional appraisal or motor priming, without explicit awareness. These combined challenges can negatively affect coping, daily functioning, and engagement with both psychological and somatic care. At the same time, mental health problems are not always adequately identified or treated, partly due to fragmentation between mental and physical healthcare, resulting in limited integration of psychological support within chronic care pathways.

summary: Robotic joints are indispensable components that directly determine the capabilities and performance of diverse robotic systems. Current approaches employ soft actuators, variable stiffness mechanisms, and compliant transmission elements to enhance safety and operational efficiency. On the other hand, industrial robots necessitate joint designs that prioritize high precision, repeatability, and robustness. The intricate design of these joints balances compactness, reliability, and a broad spectrum of functional prerequisites, necessitating a multidisciplinary synthesis of expertise in mechanics, actuation systems, control algorithms, and materials science to deploy joints that not only function precisely but also adapt effectively to the specific demands of different robotic tasks.

title: Stratification and Predictive Biomarkers in Autism and Other Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Advancing EEG and Eye-Tracking Approaches to Optimize Intervention Strategies
summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are characterized by substantial heterogeneity in etiology, symptomatology, developmental course, and treatment response. This heterogeneity poses significant challenges for clinical practice and research, particularly in the design and evaluation of effective early interventions. Attempts to stratify children diagnosed with these conditions have been primarily based on behavioral criteria, but clinical subtyping operates without reference to the underlying neurobiological mechanisms and has limited predictive value of the forthcoming developmental path. To advance tailored interventions in ASD and other NDDs, there is a growing emphasis on the discovery and validation of biomarkers that can objectively identify clinically meaningful subgroups and predict intervention response.

summary: Neurological disorders represent a highly complex area within medicine, characterized by multifactorial etiologies involving disruptions across numerous genes, molecular pathways, and brain networks. title: Beyond the "Gold Standard": Improvements and Advancements in Autism Diagnosis
summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) continues to be one of the most intricate and diverse neurodevelopmental disorders, exhibiting considerable diversity among individuals and settings. Despite the use of "gold-standard" diagnostic tools like the ADOS-2, current diagnostic methods face several challenges; such as false negatives, issues with ecological validity and difficulties in diagnosis in individuals with comorbid conditions. Alongside this, additional factors such as masking and camouflaging confound the clinical picture, sometimes obscuring symptoms until later in life. However, diagnostic methods specifically tailored for adults remain more limited compared to the established tools available for children. To improve the accuracy and timeliness of diagnoses, it is crucial to address these diagnostic limitations.

title: Current Perspectives of The Neurobiology of Prosody and Rhythm
summary: Prosody and rhythm are core components of speech that allow the brain to transform acoustic signals into linguistic and affective meaning. The interplay of pitch, stress, timing, and intonation patterns conveys syntactic structure, emotion, and communicative intent, while rhythmic organization supports segmentation, prediction, and motor coordination. Recent neuroscience research has revealed that prosodic and rhythmic functions depend on distributed neural networks spanning auditory, motor, subcortical, and cerebellar regions, coordinated by oscillatory activity across temporal scales. Despite these advances, key questions remain about how these systems develop, how their dysfunction contributes to communication disorders, and how prosody interacts with music, movement, and emotion across contexts and languages. Bridging these knowledge gaps is essential to understand how the brain encodes the temporal and melodic contours that shape human speech.

title: Know your rodent: Impact of rodent strain on learning, memory, cognition and animal models of brain disease
summary: The choice of rodent strain for neuroscientific research is often considered a secondary factor when selecting rat or mouse models for functional studies of the brain. The predominant backstrain for transgenic mice is the C57BL/6 mouse strain, which is also the most widely used strain in non-transgenic experiments. However, this mouse strain develops progressive deafness beginning in early postnatal life and also exhibits a variety of ocular dysfunctions that may influence behavioral outcomes. Other mouse strains display marked differences in learning propensity, emotionality, and cognitive performance, as well as variability in both the behavioral symptoms and mechanistic underpinnings of disease models. A similar pattern is observed in rats, whereby, for example, Albino strains exhibit differences in learning compared to pigmented rat strains, that may be associated with differences in excitation-inhibition balance derives from altered GABAergic regulation.

title: Innovative electrode and bioelectronic technologies for neural recording and stimulation
summary: Neuroengineering is an ever-evolving field that is transforming our understanding of the nervous system through the development of sophisticated electrode and bioelectronic technologies. Traditional neural electrodes face significant challenges in interface stability, biocompatibility, long-term signal fidelity, and resolution, which hinder their broader application in neuroscience research and brain–machine interfacing. Recent studies have introduced innovations such as flexible materials, nano-scale architectures, and minimally invasive designs that promise higher integration with neural tissues, reduced immune response, and improved longevity. Despite these advances, achieving seamless, durable, and high-resolution communication with neural circuits remains one of the central challenges in next-generation neural interfacing.

title: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to devastating and often irreversible loss of sensory and motor function due to the limited regenerative capacity of the adult central nervous system. Axon regeneration, the ability of injured neurons to re-extend functional projections, is a critical prerequisite for restoring connectivity and neurological recovery. Despite decades of research, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern axon regeneration remain only partially understood. This Research Topic aims to highlight emerging molecular and cellular targets that drive axon regeneration following spinal cord injury. By integrating discoveries from transcriptomic profiling, genetic manipulation, and advanced imaging, this collection seeks to uncover new regulatory pathways and therapeutic strategies that promote axonal growth and synaptic reconnection after injury.

summary: Neuroimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, and autoimmune encephalitis, are debilitating conditions characterized by an aberrant immune response against the nervous system. This has left a substantial unmet need for many patients. The field is now undergoing a transformation with the introduction of targeted therapies, including monoclonal antibodies against specific immune molecules (e.g., CD20, complement proteins) and small molecule inhibitors. These novel agents promise greater efficacy and precision. Furthermore, next-generation approaches like bispecific antibodies and CAR-T cell therapy are emerging, pushing the boundaries of precision medicine in neurology.

title: CNS demyelinating diseases: from biology to translational medicine
summary: Demyelinating diseases of the central nervous system (CNS), including multiple sclerosis (MS) and related inflammatory and degenerative disorders, represent a major cause of neurological disability worldwide. title: Recent Advances in the Stabilization and Integration of Associative Memories
summary: The potential to adapt our behavior in response to environmental demands relies on our ability to generate and update memories of relevant information. After learning, memories undergo consolidation, a process that strengthens memory traces and transforms them into stable, long-lasting forms. On a cellular level, learning triggers rapid posttranslational modifications, such as the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins, facilitating synapse formation and maturation. On the circuit level, various brain areas form networks crucial for learning and memory. The most studied is the one involving the hippocampus, neocortex, and limbic nuclei, which are essential for memory consolidation. According to system consolidation theory, memories are initially encoded by the hippocampus and later transferred to the neocortex. This idea has been backed by studies that reveal coordination between hippocampal reactivations and cortical oscillations during sleep.

title: Imaging-Guided Neuromodulation for Brain Cognitive Function Enhancement: Methodological Advances in Targeting, Biomarkers, and Validation
summary: Neuroimaging has become central to cognitive enhancement research, transforming non-invasive neuromodulation from an empirical practice into a mechanistically grounded discipline. Today, neuroregulatory technologies — including transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), TMS, neurofeedback, and emerging modalities such as tFUS and TIS — are routinely paired with fMRI, fNIRS, and EEG. This coupling shifts cognitive enhancement from behavioral observation toward mechanistic exploration: imaging defines cortical targets, monitors interventions in real time, and validates stimulation effects at the network level. Yet critical methodological gaps remain. Artifact contamination in simultaneous stimulation–imaging recordings, multi-site inconsistencies, limited reliability of imaging biomarkers, and weak causal links between stimulation, imaging changes, and cognitive outcomes all constrain reproducibility and individualization.

summary: Predictive Coding (PC) is a prominent theoretical framework that posits that a core function of the brain is a hierarchical inference process. It actively generates predictions about the causes of sensory input and continuously updates these based on "prediction errors" (the mismatch between expectation and reality). This parsimonious model offers a mechanistic account for a wide range of typical cognitive functions, from basic sensory inference and perceptual stability to motor control and decision-making.

summary: The integration of immersive virtual reality (IVR) in educational contexts marks a substantial shift in learning environments, offering high sensory fidelity and interactive potential. However, as students transition from traditional physical classrooms to virtual settings, they frequently encounter the “Transposition Challenge,” losing access to familiar self-regulatory supports such as notes, clocks, and peer cues. This regulatory void, or “regulatory nakedness,” can elevate extraneous cognitive load and disrupt emotional equilibrium, hindering both engagement and learning outcomes. Recent work—guided by models such as the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) and the Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media for VR (CATLM-VR)—underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of how immersion, embodiment, and interactivity modulate core learning variables including presence, interest, cognitive load, and motivation.

title: Digital Mental Health for People with Chronic Conditions: experiences, impact and interventions
summary: About 60% of people live with a chronic illness, such as eczema, epilepsy or a cleft lip. This ranges from 25% in children to 96% in people aged 75 and older. A chronic illness is defined as a condition that lasts longer than three months, recurs more than three times a year and/or is related to long-term use of medication, treatment or help (van Hal et al., 2019). According to the WHO, chronic conditions are conditions that require ongoing management over a period of years or decades. Living with a chronic illness often involves facing recurrent or long-term physical health issues, frequent medical treatment, and ongoing medication use. These experiences, alongside social and psychological stressors, contribute to an elevated risk of mental health difficulties, including depression, anxiety, and body image concerns.

Advances in brain-computer interfaces: adaptive decoding, real-world applications, and neural data augmentation
summary: Research on Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) stands at the intersection of neuroscience, engineering, and artificial intelligence, aiming to bridge communication between the brain and external devices. Despite major strides in the technical feasibility of BCIs, especially regarding neural signal acquisition and interface hardware, significant obstacles persist in translating laboratory advancements to real-world use. Key limitations include the adaptability of decoding algorithms to dynamic environments, the robustness of BCIs in daily life scenarios, and the challenges posed by limited or noisy neural data. Recent studies highlight the emerging importance of adaptive decoding—where algorithms learn and adjust to individual and contextual changes—and neural data augmentation techniques that compensate for sparse or imperfect datasets, both of which are critical for improving BCI reliability outside controlled settings.

title: Improving decoding of neuroinformation: towards the diversity of neural engineer, Volume II
summary: The Central Nervous System (CNS) provides information about how individuals collect information from their surroundings, how they process that information to make decisions, and finally, how they behave and act in their environment. CNS information can be gathered from three main sources: (1) electrical currents (e.g., electroencephalography – EEG) or electrocorticography (ECoG)), (2) magnetic fields (e.g., magnetoencephalography – MEG), and (3) level of blood oxygen or blood flow (e.g., functional near infrared spectroscopy – NIRS or functional magnetic resonance imaging – fMRI). This neuroinformation is being decoded to develop neural interfaces that aim to establish, re-establish and/or improve the neural interconnectivity of CNS in order to optimize the human-environment interaction. Not only decoding of neuroinformation has been pursued so far, but also finding the best way to recode neuroinformation by brain stimulation has been of interest in the scientific community.

title: Interactions between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems in brain health
summary: Brain health is the result of intricate communication between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems. Traditionally, these systems were studied in isolation; however, recent advances highlight their dynamic crosstalk and their collective influence on brain function. Neuroinflammation, hormonal signaling, and immune responses are now recognized as critical factors in neurological development, homeostasis, and disease. Disruptions in these inter-system interactions are implicated in a myriad of conditions, such as neurodegenerative diseases, psychiatric disorders, and metabolic syndromes. As our understanding deepens, there is a growing appreciation for integrative approaches that examine these systems together, offering novel insights into mechanisms underlying brain health and disease.

title: Targeting Neurodegeneration: Emerging Biomarkers, Therapeutics, and Translational Strategies with Small Molecules, Natural Compounds, and Nanotechnology
summary: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's pose major challenges due to their progressive, irreversible nature and the limited availability of effective treatments. However, recent breakthroughs in biomarker research and therapeutic innovation offer new hope. Advances in molecular and imaging biomarkers are enabling earlier diagnosis and more precise monitoring of disease progression. At the same time, the development of small molecules targeting pathogenic proteins and the exploration of bioactive natural compounds have sparked growing interest. Moreover, nanotechnology is transforming drug delivery, offering novel strategies to cross the blood-brain barrier and enhance therapeutic efficacy.

title: openEHR and the Open Platform Ecosystem: Clinical Models, Vendor-Neutral Architectures, and Collaboration Across Standards for Interoperable, Patient-Centred Care, Clinical Research
summary: Health systems worldwide face persistent fragmentation of clinical data across proprietary systems, hindering care coordination, patient safety, and the secondary use of data for research, public health, and AI. Despite decades of standardisation efforts, most electronic health record deployments remain locked into vendor-specific data models that limit semantic interoperability and long-term data portability. The open platform approach, anchored in the openEHR specifications, offers an alternative architecture based on vendor-neutral, standardised clinical models managed collaboratively by clinicians and informaticians.

title: Evidence of Off-Label Drug Use to Reduce Dementia
summary: Emerging evidence from basic, clinical, and epidemiological studies suggests that drug mechanisms of currently approved drugs can impact the risk and progression of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Repurposing existing drugs is a pathway for treatment that has worked for several other conditions (e.g., cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, erectile dysfunction) and this pathway to treatment can often be faster and more cost-effective than developing a new drug and going through the process to market approval. As ADRD grows as a public health problem placing a huge personal and financial cost on individuals, families, and the healthcare system, harnessing effective treatment quickly is key to reducing burden. Given the expense, safety risks, and substantial patient burden to receive treatment associated with lecanemab, the only current treatment available for AD, developing safe strategies for easier treatment is necessary.

summary: The field of neurocardiology explores the intricate, bidirectional communications between the brain and the heart-collectively termed the Brain-Heart Axis. This multifaceted network encompasses neural, autonomic, endocrine, immune, and metabolic signaling pathways responsible for maintaining physiological balance. Recent advances underscore that disruptions in the brain-heart axis can significantly contribute to a spectrum of disorders such as autonomic cardiomyopathy, neurodegenerative disease-linked cardiac complications, stroke, and stress-related cardiomyopathies. Despite considerable mechanistic insights into the neurocardiac interface, key questions remain regarding the translation of these findings to clinical practice, the full repertoire of signaling networks involved, and the development of specific biomarkers and targeted interventions.

summary: Neurocritical care has evolved into a discipline with clear benefits, with organised services linked to lower mortality and better functional outcomes. title: Predictive motor control and internal models
summary: Skilled motor behaviour relies on the central nervous system’s capacity to predict, rather than merely react to, the sensory consequences of its own actions. From reaching for a cup of coffee to maintaining balance on a moving train, every voluntary movement relies on the central nervous system’s ability to anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions. This predictive capacity is thought to be supported by internal models: neural representations of the body and the external world that allow the brain to estimate forthcoming states and select appropriate motor commands. Forward models predict the sensory outcomes of motor actions, while inverse models compute the motor commands required to achieve a desired sensory or kinematic goal. Together, they form the computational backbone of skilled, flexible, and adaptive behaviour, and their disruption is increasingly recognised as a hallmark of several neurological and psychiatric conditions.

title: Lipid Signaling in Neurological Disorders: From Neurodegeneration to Neuroinflammation
summary: The brain is composed of approximately 60% to 70% lipids, which primarily serve as structural components. However, many of these lipids also play critical roles in cellular signaling. In particular, sphingolipids and lysophospholipids function as second messengers, direct receptor ligands, and/or metabolic intermediates in various signaling pathways. Intracellularly, lysophospholipids serve as intermediate precursors for the biosynthesis of other lipids, whereas extracellular lysophospholipids act as signaling molecules that mediate diverse physiological processes. Dysregulation of sphingolipid and lysophospholipid metabolism has been increasingly associated with the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis, suggesting that lipid signaling plays a pivotal role in neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal survival.

Decoding Neurodegeneration: Insights into the Pathways of Neurological Decline
summary: Neurodegeneration is the gradual and progressive loss of neuron function and structure that ultimately leads to neuronal death. This phenomenon underlies a spectrum of debilitating disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The hallmark of neurodegeneration is the aggregation of misfolded proteins, such as amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles in Alzheimer's or alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, which disrupt cellular processes and trigger neuroinflammatory responses. Mitochondrial dysfunction is another critical factor, as impaired energy production and increased oxidative stress contribute to neuronal damage and apoptosis.

title: From Genetic Risk to Targeted Treatment in Neurodegenerative Disorders
summary: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, constitute a primary global health concern due to their progressive, debilitating, and currently incurable nature. These diseases arise from extensive neuronal degeneration, impairing motor, cognitive, and autonomic functions. Advances in molecular biology and genomics have catalyzed a paradigm shift from symptomatic treatment to mechanistic understanding, emphasizing the etiological role of genetic factors. Central to this shift is the emerging utility of genetic signatures—distinctive gene expression profiles that reflect underlying pathogenic processes. These signatures include coordinated transcriptional changes across gene networks, offering enhanced resolution over single-gene analyses. summary: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as potential early indicators and modifiable risk factors for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD). Disruptions in sleep, circadian rhythms, and specific sleep disorders (e.g., sleep apnea, insomnia, REM sleep behavior disorder) are common in older adults and have been linked to accelerated amyloid-beta accumulation, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and impaired glymphatic clearance, all key hallmarks of ADRD. Given the long preclinical phase of ADRD and the urgent need for early intervention strategies, identifying reliable and non-invasive predictive biomarkers is of high clinical significance.

title: Neurobiological mediators of clinical outcomes in psychedelic-assisted therapies
summary: Psychedelic-assisted therapies have demonstrated rapid and often sustained clinical benefit across depression, PTSD, and other conditions. Neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and molecular studies increasingly link these effects to structural and functional neuroplasticity, supported by theoretical frameworks such as the Entropic Brain Hypothesis and REBUS. In parallel, clinical and qualitative research emphasizes the centrality of the subjective, phenomenological experience to therapeutic outcome. These two literatures — neurobiological and phenomenological — have largely developed in parallel, with few studies directly testing how they relate within the same patient sample. Consequently, whether neurobiological changes are causally responsible for clinical improvement, merely predictive of it, or simply co-occurring alongside a distinct psychological process remains an open and clinically consequential question.

title: Fluid Biomarkers in Neurodegeneration: Revolutionizing Early Detection and Prognosis
summary: Over the past decade, fluid biomarkers have transformed the conceptual and clinical framework of neurodegenerative diseases. In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) measures of amyloid-β peptides, phosphorylated tau, and total tau, together with emerging blood-based biomarkers such as plasma p-tau isoforms, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial markers, have moved from research settings toward clinical implementation. This shift has enabled the transition from a purely syndromic diagnosis to a biologically defined disease model, as reflected in the AT(N) framework. The AD model demonstrates that neurodegeneration can be detected years before clinical symptoms emerge, opening new opportunities for early intervention and disease-modifying therapies. Importantly, this paradigm is now extending beyond AD, influencing biomarker research in other neurodegenerative disorders related to aging, including Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and atypical parkinsonism

Under homeostatic conditions (notably during brain development), complement contributes to synaptic refinement and clearance of cellular debris. In contrast, chronic or dysregulated complement activation in CNS injury or disease drives neuroinflammation, synapse loss, and neurodegeneration. These effects have been characterized across numerous conditions, including Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), Spinal Cord Injury (SCI), Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), Stroke, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Multiple Sclerosis (MS), and others. Neuroactive microbial metabolites and human brain function: mechanisms, biomarkers, and clinical implications
summary: In the rapidly evolving field of neurogastroenterology, mounting evidence highlights the profound influence of neuroactive microbial metabolites on human brain function. The gut-brain axis has become a focal point for understanding how metabolites produced by gut microbiota, reshaped by factors such as diet, medications, and stress, interact with the central nervous system. Recent studies have delineated pathways by which short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, bile acids, and other molecules alter blood–brain barrier integrity, microglial activation, neurotransmitter systems, and neural connectivity. Despite promising insights, critical questions remain regarding the reproducibility of findings, individual susceptibility, and translation to clinical practice. There remains a significant gap in mapping specific metabolite signatures to neuropsychiatric phenotypes, as well as understanding how genetic and environmental factors modulate these effects.

summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven computational modeling have opened unprecedented opportunities to transform diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-making, and outcome prediction across the field of orthopedic surgery. The musculoskeletal system exhibits highly complex biomechanical behavior, nonlinear tissue responses, and substantial inter-patient variability, all of which challenge the effectiveness of conventional clinical assessment methods. summary: Embodiment in cognition, language, and communication examines how sensorimotor systems intertwine with language comprehension, suggesting that even the understanding of abstract expressions may be rooted in physical experience (Barsalou, 2010). Cognitive neuroscience and psychology studies reveal that metaphorical language activates brain areas associated with perception and action, underscoring the impact of embodied experiences on conceptual structures (D’Angiulli, Griffiths, & Marmolejo-Ramos, 2015). Recognizing language's embodied nature is crucial; it is entwined with sensory, motor, and affective experiences, and structured through metaphorical mappings (Khatin-Zadeh & Vahdat, 2015).

summary: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) remains the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, yet it continues to evade a definitive disease-modifying therapy (DMT). Despite extensive research over the past decades, no single clinical trial has succeeded in demonstrating a treatment capable of altering the disease's course. This ongoing challenge is linked to several complexities in PD, such as an incomplete comprehension of its pathophysiology, an elongated prodromal stage, the absence of validated biomarkers of progression, substantial clinical phenotype heterogeneity with considerable symptom variability, and high concurrence of co-pathology. These issues pose significant methodological obstacles for DMTs, including the design and duration of trials, correct patient stratification, therapeutic candidate selection, the development of valid, specific, and sensitive clinical outcome measures, and surrogate biomarkers.

Visually Guided Walking in Complex Environments: Neural, Biomechanical, and Translational Insights for Neuroprosthetics
summary: Walking is a deceptively complex behavior. Each step depends on the continuous integration of visual input, vestibular and proprioceptive signals, and motor commands distributed across cortical, subcortical, and spinal circuits. Vision plays a particularly central role: it anticipates obstacles, calibrates foot placement, and tunes locomotor control before the foot contacts the ground. When this visuomotor loop is disrupted by injury, neurological disease, aging, limb loss, or the use of a prosthetic or exoskeletal device, gait becomes slower, more variable, and metabolically costly. Mobile brain/body imaging (MoBI) including high-density EEG, fNIRS, EMG, inertial sensors, and motion capture, enables in-situ measurement of the brain and body during complex realistic behaviours. These advances have direct implications for neuroprosthetics: powered prostheses, exoskeletons, and brain–machine interfaces must ultimately operate inside the user’s own visuomotor control loop.

summary: Subjectively and phenomenologically, sexual arousal is a state of pleasure, joy, passion, and bodily excitement, followed by delight, positive exhaustion, and relaxation. Biologically, it involves changes in physiological arousal, the release of hormones and neurotransmitters in the autonomic nervous system and the central nervous system. In dimensional biological emotion theories, it represents the highly positive endpoint in the affective space defined by valence and physiological arousal, triggered by internal or external pleasurable and erotic stimuli. From an evolutionary perspective, the purpose of sexual arousal and pleasure is to prime action disposition for approach or avoidance, thereby supporting survival and driving perceptual, cognitive, and emotional resources through motivational systems that prioritize mating and influence decision-making about sexual behaviors.

title: MicroRNA dysregulation and Apolipoprotein E in sporadic Alzheimer’s disease: molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and sex-specific effects
summary: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) accounts for 60–80% of all dementia cases, with women at higher risk due to both longevity and biological factors. Familial AD, caused by mutations in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2, represents less than 5% of cases, whereas sporadic AD (>90%) is mainly associated with polymorphisms in APOE and TREM2, which influence amyloid beta (Aβ) clearance. The APOE4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic AD, yet the precise role of Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) in disease pathogenesis is still not fully understood.

summary: Stress and memory research continues to uncover the intricate and often paradoxical ways in which stressors influence memory processes. While numerous studies highlight how stress-related hormones can enhance memory consolidation yet impair retrieval, the underlying evolutionary and adaptive roles of these mechanisms remain somewhat elusive. This field's complexity is amplified by the cross-species insights into these processes and the varied outcomes dependent on factors such as stress intensity, memory phase, and learning context. Despite progress in understanding neuromodulators' roles in emotional memory, there is still a considerable challenge in predicting a memory's outcome—whether it will be strengthened, weakened, or inhibited—following a stressful event.

summary: Artificial intelligence is now being investigated across much of clinical neurology, including EEG interpretation, seizure detection, stroke imaging, neurodegenerative disease classification, neurocritical care monitoring, and clinical decision support. Many studies report high performance using metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or area under the ROC curve. Yet the number of systems with robust evidence of real-world clinical benefit remains comparatively small. This translational gap reflects recurrent methodological and implementation problems: reliance on narrowly characterized public datasets, limited demographic and technical diversity, insufficient external validation, incomplete calibration assessment, and evaluation strategies that do not map onto clinically meaningful decisions.

title: How Does the Environment Modulate Feeding and Metabolism in Fish? Special Emphasis on the Impacts of Climate Change
summary: Feeding and metabolism in fish are vital physiological processes regulated by interactions between internal endocrine signals and external environmental cues. Fish are highly sensitive to environmental parameters such as temperature, oxygen availability, salinity, photoperiod, pollution, and food quality. These variables influence feeding behavior, nutrient assimilation, and energy allocation. The regulation of these functions involves an endocrine network that integrates signals from the brain, gut, liver, and adipose tissue. Hormones such as neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), CART, orexin, leptin, ghrelin, insulin, thyroid hormones, melanocortins, and insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) play central roles in modulating appetite and metabolism.

title: Resource‑ and Energy‑Aware Multi‑Robot Operations: Scheduling, Recharging, and Long‑Horizon Persistence
summary: Battery capacity, recharge logistics, and computational budgets are now the primary bottlenecks for scaling multi robot systems from short demos to dependable, 24/7 operations. Long horizon missions—warehousing, inspection, agriculture, environmental monitoring, and public safety—require fleets to coordinate tasks, routes, and recharge events while accounting for battery aging, stochastic demand, uncertain travel times, and heterogeneous platforms. Classical planning or perception advances alone are insufficient: persistence hinges on resource models, predictive energy usage, and infrastructure aware scheduling that closes the loop between algorithms, chargers, and the physical environment. This Research Topic focuses on the algorithmic and systems foundations that make multi robot autonomy sustainable and economically viable over days to months, emphasizing measurable mission availability, throughput, safety under energy constraints, and total cost of ownership.

Affective Computing Meets Embodied Intelligence: Emotion Perception, Reasoning, and Interaction in Embodied Agents
summary: Affective computing aims to endow machines with the ability to recognize, interpret, and respond to human emotions, while embodied intelligence emphasizes that cognition emerges through an agent's physical interaction with its environment. Historically, these two fields have advanced along largely separate trajectories: affective computing has focused on emotion recognition from facial, vocal, physiological, and textual signals, whereas embodied intelligence has concentrated on perception, control, and manipulation in the physical world. Recent breakthroughs in large multimodal models, foundation models for robotics, and human-robot interaction have created unprecedented opportunities to unify the two. Emotion is no longer treated as a passive signal to be classified, but as an active component that shapes how embodied agents perceive, reason, decide, and act within dynamic, socially rich environments.

title: Cognitive–motor interactions in aging: neural mechanisms, behavioral signatures, and functional consequences
summary: The fields of motor control and cognitive psychology have been traditionally separate, but research has fundamentally reshaped this distinction. We now understand that motor control and cognitive functions are inextricably linked, sharing neural pathways and competing for limited resources, especially in aging. As neural efficiency declines in aging, there is a tradeoff between using resources to support motor performance and cognitive function. For example, older adults often display reduced performance on complex tasks due to cognitive-motor interference, compared to younger adults. Understanding the mechanisms behind this shift is critical for distinguishing between healthy aging and early-stage neurodegeneration. It will also facilitate the development of interventions aimed at preserving functional independence.

title: Advances in MRI Radiomics for Non-Invasive Glioma Assessment
summary: Glioma research has rapidly evolved in recent years, particularly in the context of diagnostic imaging and personalized medicine. Gliomas, representing the most prevalent malignant primary brain tumors, are remarkably heterogeneous, posing significant challenges for classification, treatment, and prognosis. While magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains indispensable for diagnosing and monitoring gliomas, traditional visual assessments are often insufficient to uncover the full spectrum of tumor heterogeneity and correlate with underlying molecular features. With advances in computational methods, MRI radiomics has emerged as a transformative approach by extracting large sets of quantitative features from routine imaging, promising to bridge the gap between imaging phenotypes and the molecular landscape of brain tumors.

title: Adaptive immune involvement in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and related dementias
summary: The intersection of neuroimmunology and neurodegeneration has advanced considerably in recent years, with particular interest focused on the role of the adaptive immune system in disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and related dementias. Significant studies have revealed correlations between adaptive immune cell infiltration, neuroinflammation, and disease pathology in both human samples and animal models. For example, T cell reactivity against alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta has been observed in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's patients, respectively, while emerging data suggest that autoimmune reactions may exacerbate or modulate disease trajectories. This evolving landscape indicates a pressing need for deeper mechanistic understanding, as well as clarification of the specific immune signatures and pathways involved in diverse patient populations.

title: NeuroAI and the brain: Integrating brain-inspired computational models and large-scale AI architectures with computational theories of neural function
summary: The rapid ascent of large-scale artificial intelligence has provided neuroscience with a new set of powerful tools for modeling complex cognitive functions. Historically, computational neuroscience has balanced between biophysically detailed models of single neurons and abstract, small-scale circuit motifs. However, the ability of modern AI to perform human-like tasks in sensory processing, motor control, and linguistics offers a "top-down" framework to understand how the brain might organize high-dimensional data. This convergence, known as NeuroAI, suggests that the representational spaces of deep networks can serve as predictive scaffolds for neural activity. Despite this potential, a critical gap remains: most AI models lack the biological constraints, metabolic efficiency, and architectural diversity of the brain, while many neural models struggle to scale to the complexity of real-world behavior.

Modeling Sensory Encoding: Computational Approaches to Feature Detection, Integration, and Adaptation
summary: Sensory encoding is the vital process by which the nervous system transforms physical stimuli into meaningful neural representations. Traditionally, computational neuroscience has characterized this through receptive fields and stimulus-response functions. However, sensory systems do not operate in a vacuum; they must extract relevant features from high-dimensional, noisy environments while constantly adjusting to changing contexts. From the retina’s light adaptation to the auditory system’s frequency tuning, the brain employs sophisticated computational strategies to ensure efficient information transmission. As our ability to record from large sensory populations grows, we are moving beyond simple linear models toward theories that encompass non-linear dynamics, population-level interactions, and the influence of feedback. Understanding these principles is essential for deciphering how the brain constructs a coherent internal map of the external world.

Alzheimer's disease-associated genes expression: A new direction in the ischemic etiology and therapy of Alzheimer's disease
summary: Increasing evidence supports a link between brain ischemia and the development of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Experimental and clinical studies have shown that ischemic episodes trigger the overexpression of genes associated with AD pathology, including amyloid precursor protein (APP), β-secretase (BACE1), presenilin 1 and 2, and tau protein. These changes promote beta-amyloid peptide accumulation, neurofibrillary tangle formation, and progressive neurodegeneration in patterns that closely mirror the hallmarks of AD. Despite growing recognition that ischemia-reperfusion injury may represent a critical upstream trigger for AD-type pathology, the molecular cascades linking ischemic gene dysregulation to sustained neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood. This gap limits the development of targeted therapies that could intervene at the vascular and ischemic level to slow or prevent the onset of AD.

title: Advances in perceptual intelligence for autonomous robotic systems
summary: Perceptual intelligence is a foundational pillar in robotics, enabling autonomous systems to interact safely and effectively with complex, dynamic environments. Recent advances in biological and engineered perception highlight the remarkable adaptability, efficiency, and resilience seen in nature and underscore the gains possible through interdisciplinary innovation. While bio-inspired models offer critical insights for embodied perception and action, robotics research today increasingly benefits from data-driven algorithms, hybrid methodologies, and novel sensor designs that extend beyond traditional paradigms. Ongoing research debates the relative merits of symbolic versus sub-symbolic learning, the integration of diverse sensory modalities, and strategies for achieving interpretability and transparency in robotic decisions—factors of growing importance as robots take on roles in mission-critical and socially interactive domains.

Neurovascular Inflammation in Aneurysm Pathogenesis and Its Contribution to Neurodegenerative Processes
summary: Neurovascular inflammation represents a critical area of research in understanding the dynamics of aneurysm formation and rupture, known precursors to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and subsequent cerebral vasospasm. These events can lead to secondary neuronal injury, highlighting an important connection to neurodegenerative processes. Pathological neuroinflammation has emerged as a primary driver in these mechanisms, where initial endothelial damage - precipitated by factors like hypertension, genetic predispositions, or lifestyle choices such as smoking - initiates maladaptive vascular inflammation. This cascade involves monocyte infiltration and cytokine release, notably IL-6, which compromises vessel integrity and encourages aneurysmal expansion and rupture.

title: Targeting Neuroinflammation: Mechanisms, Pathways and Therapeutic Opportunities
summary: Neuroinflammation is a critical pathological process at the intersection of immunology and neuroscience. It is now established as a key driver in the onset and progression of a wide range of central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, and depression. The complex interplay between activated glial cells, inflammatory signaling, and neuronal function presents both a significant challenge and a compelling opportunity for therapeutic intervention. Despite significant advances in understanding these mechanisms, effective pharmacological treatments targeting neuroinflammation remain scarce outside of broad immunosuppressive approaches.

Molecular Mechanisms Linking Circadian Rhythm Disruption to Neurological and Neuropsychiatric Disorders
summary: Within the field of molecular neuroscience, circadian rhythms are increasingly recognized as fundamental regulators of brain health and disease. Disruption of these intrinsic biological clocks has been closely linked with a spectrum of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, major depression, and schizophrenia. Recent studies have begun to unravel how circadian dysfunction can influence brain pathology through mechanisms such as altered gene expression, synaptic activity, neuroinflammation, and impaired neuronal communication. Despite these advances, significant questions remain about the precise molecular pathways involved, the degree to which circadian disruption drives disease onset versus exacerbating existing pathology, and how these processes differ between individuals and disease types. There is a clear need for further integrative research to clarify these mechanisms and resolve ongoing debates in the field.

Edge-AI addresses this by moving perception and decision-making closer to the sensor, reducing latency and bandwidth demands while enabling real-time response in the field. Exploring oxytocin as a neuroendocrine integrator
summary: Oxytocin has been the subject of much research that has greatly expanded our understanding of its role in integrating brain-body interactions. Recent evidence identifies oxytocin as a critical modulator within the gut-brain-endocrine axis, regulating neuroendocrine and neuroimmune signaling pathways in both bottom-up (gut-to-brain) and top-down (brain-to-gut) directions. While oxytocin concentrations in the central brain are approximately three orders of magnitude higher than peripheral blood concentration, oxytocin receptors are widely distributed across many peripheral tissues. Indeed, recent studies have pointed to associations between oxytocin and gut microbiota-derived metabolites, vagal afferent signaling and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity, positioning oxytocin as a key modulator of metabolic and endocrine signals.

title: Realistic multi-scale modeling of neural circuit dynamics - Volume II
summary: We are pleased to announce this Volume II Research Topic, building upon the impactful contributions and insightful discussions generated by the first Research Topic in this series - 'Realistic Multi-Scale Modeling of Neural Circuit Dynamics'. Neural circuit dynamics remain profoundly complex, underpinned by intricate interactions spanning molecular, cellular, and network scales. While significant advancements in computational neuroscience have enabled the development of increasingly detailed biophysical models, the fundamental challenge persists: effectively bridging these disparate scales to achieve truly comprehensive and predictive simulations. This ongoing endeavor is crucial for advancing our understanding of brain function and dysfunction, necessitating continued exploration and innovation in multi-scale modeling approaches.

title: Collaborative Approaches to Addressing Violent Extremism in Practice
summary: Efforts to prevent and address violent extremism have been a central focus for NGOs, institutes, and agencies operating outside of academia and government. These organizations, such as the Radicalisation Awareness Network (RAN), often operate on behalf of local governments and play a crucial role in shaping policies, programs, and networks aimed at tackling the issue. Despite their central position in managing trends and developments, their experiences and knowledge are relatively underrepresented in academic discussions. This gap represents a missed opportunity to leverage experiences and knowledge by combining scholarly understanding with practical insights from the frontlines of extremism prevention.

title: Global Challenges in Brain Banking for Neurology Research
summary: Exploration of human brain tissue is pivotal for advancing neurology and improving public health, especially as the world faces a growing health crisis linked to the aging population and associated neurodegenerative diseases. Traditional animal models fall short in mirroring human brain pathophysiology, necessitating the use of human post-mortem specimens to thoroughly investigate brain functions and mechanisms under both normal and pathological states. The development of brain banks—facilities that collect, store, and manage brain specimens—in different ethnic-geographical contexts and the sharing of protocols and information are critical to support the evolution of "precision neurology," which aims to integrate clinicopathological data with genomic and other omics-based methodologies to illuminate the causes of brain diseases.

Microglial Dynamics in Alzheimer's: Genetic Variants and Therapeutic Pathways
summary: Microglia are pivotal players in the neuroinflammatory landscape of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Accumulating evidence underscores their complex role in modulating amyloid plaque dynamics, neuronal integrity, and synaptic function. Recent genome-wide association and sequencing studies have revealed that the majority of AD risk loci are highly expressed in microglia. Variants in a broad network of microglial genes—including TREM2, ABI3, PLCG2, INPP5D, CD33, SPI1 and the MS4A cluster—can fundamentally alter microglial behavior and reactivity. While activated microglia may drive beneficial amyloid clearance and neuroprotective signaling, they can also contribute to pathological synaptic pruning and chronic neuroinflammation, creating a spectrum of responses that complicates our understanding of their exact role in AD pathogenesis. title: Machine Learning and Observational Data for Clinical Trial Optimization
summary: Clinical research has long rested on a familiar triad: the randomized trial, the carefully curated cohort, and the cross-sectional survey. Each has its strengths, and each has its blind spots. Trials give us causality but often at great cost and with narrow generalizability. Cohorts offer longitudinal depth but can suffer from attrition and evolving practice patterns. Surveys provide breadth and currency but limited temporal insight. For decades, these data streams have largely run in parallel, occasionally informing one another but rarely being analyzed together with the tools now at our disposal.

summary: Stem cells elicit immunomodulatory properties through surface protein expression and their secretome. These properties allow stem cells to influence the immune response, reduce neuroinflammation, and create a favorable environment for neuronal survival and repair. Many neurological and neurodegenerative conditions involve chronic or dysregulated neuroinflammation, which contributes to neuronal damage. In these diseases, activated microglia and astrocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1β), oxidative species, and other factors that exacerbate neurodegeneration. Stem cells have emerged as promising therapeutic tools due to their dual ability to promote neural regeneration and exert potent immunomodulatory effects. By restoring immune balance and supporting tissue repair, stem cells offer a multifaceted approach to treating neurodegenerative diseases with immunological components.

title: Philosophy meets neuroscience in the study of consciousness
summary: Conscious experience is central to human life, yet the processes underlying its emergence remain among the most debated questions in behavioral neuroscience. Over the past decade, the field has moved beyond simple contrasts between “conscious” and “unconscious” states toward mechanistic accounts grounded in large-scale brain dynamics, multisensory integration, and the interaction between perception, action, and self-representation. Progress has been driven by converging approaches, including computational frameworks (e.g., predictive processing and global workspace–type architectures), causal perturbation methods (such as TMS, DBS, and intracranial stimulation), and high-dimensional analyses of neural data from EEG, MEG, fMRI, and single-unit recordings. In parallel, experimental paradigms involving anesthesia, sleep, psychedelics, meditation, and disorders of consciousness have provided structured and naturalistic perturbations of subjective experience.

Dysregulated immune activity—manifested through microglial activation, cytokine release, or blood–brain barrier disruption—has been identified as a pivotal mechanism contributing to neuronal dysfunction in a wide array of neurological diseases. Alpha-Synuclein dynamics in Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Brain-aging
summary: Alpha-Synuclein is a presynaptic neuronal protein essential for vesicle trafficking and neurotransmitter release. While widely recognized for its pathological aggregation in disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies, its dynamics during the natural course of brain aging remain complex. Aging is characterized by a gradual loss of proteostatic control, synaptic efficacy, and altered cellular signaling. In this context, alpha-synuclein undergoes significant changes in expression, post-translational modification, and clearance even in the absence of overt disease. Understanding the nuanced shift from physiological function to pathological dysfunction is critical. As the global population ages, distinguishing between benign age-related changes in alpha-synuclein dynamics and those driving neurodegeneration is essential for developing early interventions and maintaining cognitive health.

Sensory-motor integration in human movement
summary: For desired and coordinated movements, the central nervous system integrates multiple sensory feedback with motor commands. Optimum integration of multi-sensory signals from visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems is vital to performing activities of daily life and is commonly compromised due to aging, neuromuscular disorders, and traumatic injuries. Compromised sensor-motor integration can potentially lead to a stability control deficiency, increased risk of falling, tremors, rigidity, and decreased hand dexterity, just to name a few. However, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms responsible for sensory-motor integration, specifically, how the central nervous system adapts to changes in environmental conditions (e.g., visual input is obstructed), physical and mental health, and cognitive status. A comprehensive study of sensory-motor integration can be beneficial to healthcare professionals, neuroscientists, and human health in general.

title: Impact of rare disease genes on neural development and function
summary: Rare disease genes, though individually uncommon, collectively account for a substantial share of neurodevelopmental disorders, and each one offers a distinct and often underappreciated window into how the nervous system is built and maintained. These genes contribute to neural development and maturation at every stage of the process, from initial tissue patterning and progenitor proliferation through to the acquisition of mature cellular and circuit properties. Understanding how disruption of a single rare disease gene can cascade into complex developmental and cognitive phenotypes offers valuable insight into the biological basis of disorders such as autism, ADHD, and other neurocognitive symptoms that may arise due to altered gene function.

title: Transforming Genitourinary Surgery Through Advanced Robotic Systems
summary: The field of genitourinary (GU) surgery has undergone a transformative shift with the integration of robotic technology, which now serves as a cornerstone for minimally invasive procedures. Over recent decades, advancements have evolved from pioneering platforms like PUMA 560 and Probot to current industry standards, exemplified by the da Vinci system. Robotic approaches have been lauded for improved dexterity, enhanced visualization, and better ergonomics for surgeons, leading to increasing adoption. Despite their technical promise, clinical debates remain around appropriate patient selection, comparative benefits over other minimally invasive modalities, and the economic implications of broader deployment. Although early evidence points to advantages such as reduced blood loss and faster recovery, critical gaps persist, including inconsistent outcome definitions, limited long-term data, and a lack of standardized benchmarks for both clinical and technical success.

title: Effort, Attention, and Arousal: Brain–Body Mechanisms for Performance in the Real World
summary: Sustained performance in high-stakes, real-world environments places extraordinary demands on the human brain and body. Effort, attention, and arousal are three tightly interwoven constructs that together govern how individuals mobilize cognitive and physiological resources to meet these demands. Nowhere is this more critical than in contexts in which humans are expected to perform in high stakes environments. For example, military personnel, first responders, and individuals of the like must maintain peak cognitive performance under conditions of extreme stress, fatigue, sensory overload, and physical exertion. Despite decades of laboratory research, the neural and peripheral mechanisms underpinning the interaction between mental effort, attentional control, and arousal remain incompletely understood — particularly in the demanding and ecologically complex environments that are present in real-world scenarios.

summary: Neurodevelopment is shaped by dynamic interactions among neural systems, behavioral functions, and environmental contexts. title: Generative AI and Multimodal Interaction in Mental Health: From Theoretical Foundations to Clinical Product Implementation
summary: The rapid emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) is catalyzing a paradigm shift in mental health research and service delivery. While traditional AI approaches in psychiatry have primarily focused on discriminative tasks such as diagnostic classification, GenAI introduces new capacities for scalable human-like interaction, personalized content generation, and the synthesis of complex multimodal data (e.g., language, voice, facial expression, and movement). These advances may create opportunities to strengthen mental health promotion, prevention, and care provision at the population level—yet the field faces two key challenges: an epistemological gap in understanding how GenAI reshapes mental health theory and constructs (e.g., digital phenotypes and risk/protective factors), and an implementation gap in translating algorithms into robust, clinically and publicly validated, equitable, and governable tools for real-world settings.

title: Neuroendocrine control of glucose homeostasis in health and disease
summary: The field of neuroendocrine control of glucose homeostasis is pivotal in understanding the complex interplay between metabolic diseases and brain disorders. These conditions, such as obesity and diabetes mellitus, significantly impact the quality of life for millions globally. The maintenance of glucose homeostasis is crucial for physiological functions, yet the precise mechanisms governing this balance remain a topic of intense debate. Recent studies suggest that the regulation of blood glucose levels involves a sophisticated interaction between hormones, neuropeptides, and neurotransmitters, primarily orchestrated by the brain, peripheral nerves, and pancreatic islets. However, the intricate communication pathways between the brain and pancreatic islets pose challenges in fully comprehending their role in glucose regulation. This gap in understanding underscores the need for innovative research to inform future clinical interventions aimed at preserving neurometabolic health.

summary: Tinnitus and hyperacusis are complex auditory perceptual conditions influenced by sensory, emotional, and cognitive factors. summary: The advent of high-density recording technologies, such as Neuropixels and large-scale calcium imaging, has provided an unprecedented look into the simultaneous activity of thousands of neurons. However, the sheer dimensionality and non-linear nature of this data pose significant challenges for interpretation. Traditional analytical methods often focus on discriminative tasks, mapping neural activity to external stimuli or behavior. In contrast, generative models, including Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Diffusion Models, offer a powerful alternative by learning the underlying statistical distribution of neural firing patterns. These AI-driven frameworks allow researchers to move beyond description, enabling the synthesis of realistic neural activity and the discovery of latent manifolds that govern brain states. By treating neural activity as a generative process, we can better understand the intrinsic logic of biological computation.

Their infiltrative growth patterns and frequent proximity to eloquent brain regions often limit the extent of safe resection. While maximal tumour resection, defined radiologically, has consistently been associated with improved outcomes, the benefit of incomplete resection remains uncertain, highlighting the need for careful, individualised surgical decision-making. title: Edge-Deployed Generative AI for Context-Aware Decision Support in Wearable Robotic Systems
summary: Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have transformed how machines interpret, reason, and communicate. At the same time, robotics research has made significant progress in edge computing, sensor fusion, and real-time perception systems, enabling deployment in dynamic and resource-constrained environments. Despite these developments, a critical gap remains in the integration of generative AI with embodied robotic systems operating at the edge, especially in wearable robotics such as smart helmets, assistive devices, and human-augmentation systems. Current research topics emphasise either cloud-based intelligence or isolated edge AI solutions, but lack a unified framework for real-time, context-aware decision support that combines perception, reasoning, and action under strict computational constraints.

Cerebral edema and the glymphatic system in traumatic brain injury
summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a significant public health concern, leading to considerable morbidity, mortality, and long-term disability across the globe. One of the major contributors to poor outcomes following TBI is cerebral edema, a secondary injury process characterized by excess accumulation of fluid in the brain parenchyma, which elevates intracranial pressure (ICP) and exacerbates neurological damage. Despite advances in the management of TBI, current therapies such as osmotherapy and decompressive craniectomy focus predominantly on controlling ICP rather than addressing the underlying mechanisms of edema. Emerging research highlights a crucial need to explore novel therapeutic strategies that directly target cerebral edema and its complex pathophysiology, as conventional approaches have not led to substantial improvements in patient outcomes.

Neuromodulatory and molecular control of plastic behaviors in simple neural systems
summary: Understanding how brains adapt to changing internal states and external environments remains a central challenge in neuroscience. Simple model systems, such as Aplysia, C. elegans, and Drosophila , have long provided powerful experimental leverage to dissect how neural circuits are modified to support behavioral plasticity. These systems offer unparalleled access to the molecular, cellular, and circuit-level mechanisms through which experience and context shape action. Critically, neuromodulatory signals, ranging from monoamines to neuropeptides, play a pivotal role in dynamically reconfiguring synaptic and network states. These modulators act through diverse molecular cascades to influence protein expression, ion channel function, synaptic release machinery, and structural plasticity. Understanding these interactions will provide a tractable window into the molecular and cellular logic of behavioral adaptation.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in cerebrovascular diseases: mechanisms and neurological consequences
summary: Mitochondria are central regulators of cellular metabolism, redox balance, and cell survival in the nervous system. In recent years, growing evidence has highlighted mitochondrial dysfunction as a critical contributor to the pathophysiology of cerebrovascular diseases, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, cerebral small vessel disease, and vascular cognitive impairment. Because neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and cerebrovascular endothelial cells have high metabolic demands and tightly regulated mitochondrial dynamics, disturbances in mitochondrial function can profoundly influence neural viability and neurovascular unit integrity during cerebrovascular injury.

summary: The co-occurrence of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) and schizophrenia has attracted increasing attention in recent years. Conversely, there is substantial evidence that children and adolescents with OCD are at increased risk of developing psychosis. summary: Mental health is increasingly recognized as both a precondition and an outcome of social development. However, global advances have been uneven, reflecting deep structural inequalities in exposure to social risks and in the capacity of welfare systems to buffer their effects. A growing body of evidence shows that mental health outcomes are strongly shaped by social policies that regulate income security, employment conditions, education, housing, human mobility, and social protection across the life course.
